chapterTitle: Christ Crucified and the Mind of Christ — The Wisdom Only the Spirit Can Reveal
themeTitle: “A Faith That Stands on a Performance Will Fall to a Better One”

scripture.text: When I came to you, brothers, I didn’t come with excellence of speech or of wisdom, proclaiming to you the testimony of God.
scripture.understanding: Paul goes back to the day he arrived. He did not come with ὑπεροχή — superiority, prominence, the elevated style of a professional orator — either of speech or of wisdom. In Corinth that was almost an insult to the audience. Rhetoric was a public entertainment, and visiting speakers were judged on their delivery the way athletes are judged on their times. Paul is reminding them that he deliberately refused to compete. What he carried was “the testimony of God” — some manuscripts read “the mystery of God” — a message he was handing on, not a performance he was giving.

scripture.text: For I determined not to know anything among you, except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.
scripture.understanding: Κρίνω — I decided, I came to a verdict. This was a decision, not a temperament. Paul could argue with philosophers (Acts 17 shows he could quote their own poets). But he resolved to know nothing among them “except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.” Not merely Christ, but Christ as the crucified one — the very part of the message Corinth would find most embarrassing. He did not lead with the least offensive truth and work up to the cross. He planted the cross at the front door.

scripture.text: I was with you in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling.
scripture.understanding: One of the most disarming admissions in Paul's letters. He came “in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling.” Ἀσθένεια, φόβος, τρόμος. He had been beaten and jailed in Philippi, chased out of Thessalonica and Berea, and mocked in Athens. Luke tells us the Lord had to speak to him in a night vision in Corinth: “Don’t be afraid, but speak and don’t be silent” (Acts 18:9). The great apostle arrived shaking. That is not a flaw in the story. It is the point of it.

scripture.text: My speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power,
scripture.understanding: Two ways to convince people. Πειθός — persuasive, the art of the enticing argument, from the same root as the Greek goddess of persuasion. Or ἀπόδειξις — a technical rhetorical term for a compelling proof, which Paul hijacks: his proof was a demonstration “of the Spirit and of power.” Paul is not anti-intellectual; Acts says he reasoned and persuaded in the synagogue every Sabbath. What he refused to do was let the result depend on his technique. The convincing was the Spirit's work.

scripture.text: that your faith wouldn’t stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God.
scripture.understanding: The purpose of the whole strategy. “That your faith wouldn’t stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God.” If Paul had argued them into it, someone cleverer could argue them out of it. A faith resting on a preacher's brilliance is only as secure as the preacher's reputation. Paul wanted their faith resting on something that could not be out-argued: an encounter with the power of God.

scripture.text: We speak wisdom, however, among those who are full grown; yet a wisdom not of this world, nor of the rulers of this world, who are coming to nothing.
scripture.understanding: But Paul is not against wisdom — he is against the wrong kind. “We speak wisdom… among those who are full grown.” Τέλειος means mature, complete, fully developed. There is real depth in the gospel, and it is for those who have grown. But it is “not of this world” — the word is αἰών, this age — and not of “the rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing.” The present participle is vivid: they are already in the process of being rendered powerless. Every empire that thinks it is permanent is passing away as you read.

scripture.text: But we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the wisdom that has been hidden, which God foreordained before the worlds for our glory,
scripture.understanding: Μυστήριον in the New Testament does not mean something mysterious that nobody can understand. It means a secret that God kept hidden and has now chosen to reveal. This wisdom was ἀποκρύπτω — hidden away — and προορίζω — marked out in advance, before the ages. And it was planned “for our glory.” Before the universe existed, God had already designed the way He would bring you into glory. You were on His mind before the world was.

scripture.text: which none of the rulers of this world has known. For had they known it, they wouldn’t have crucified the Lord of glory.
scripture.understanding: The rulers of this age did not understand it — and the proof is that they crucified “the Lord of glory.” It is one of the most explosive titles in the New Testament: the One who hung naked and bleeding on a Roman cross was the Lord to whom all glory belongs. Who are “the rulers”? At the human level, certainly Pilate, Herod, Caiaphas and the Sanhedrin (compare Acts 3:17, “you did this in ignorance, as did also your rulers”). Many interpreters also hear the spiritual powers behind them. Either way the point is the same: the powers that crucified Jesus walked straight into God's plan and did not see it.

scripture.text: But as it is written, “Things which an eye didn’t see, and an ear didn’t hear, which didn’t enter into the heart of man, these God has prepared for those who love him.”
scripture.understanding: This verse is constantly quoted at funerals as a description of heaven — but read the next verse. Paul draws on Isaiah 64:4 (blended with phrases from elsewhere in Isaiah) to describe what no human eye, ear or heart could discover by its own means: what God has prepared for those who love Him. And verse 10 says God has revealed it — already, now, by His Spirit. The verse is not mainly about what you will see after you die. It is about what you can know now that you could never have discovered without God showing you.

scripture.text: But to us, God revealed them through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, yes, the deep things of God.
scripture.understanding: “But to us, God revealed them.” Ἀποκαλύπτω — to take the cover off. And the One who takes the cover off is the Spirit, who ἐρευνάω — searches, investigates, explores — “all things, yes, the deep things of God.” Βάθος is the word for the depths of the sea. The Holy Spirit is not a force that gives you good feelings. He is a Person who knows the bottom of the ocean of God, and He is the One who teaches you.

scripture.text: For who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man, which is in him? Even so, no one knows the things of God, except God’s Spirit.
scripture.understanding: An analogy anyone can feel. Nobody really knows what is going on inside you except your own spirit. Others can guess from your face, but only you know your thoughts. In the same way, only God's Spirit knows the things of God. Which means that no amount of human research, intellect or religious effort can get inside God's mind from the outside. God has to open it from the inside.

scripture.text: But we received, not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit which is from God, that we might know the things that were freely given to us by God.
scripture.understanding: Two spirits and two worldviews. “The spirit of the world” is the prevailing mindset of the age — what everybody assumes. “The Spirit which is from God” is the Holy Spirit, given so that “we might know the things that were freely given to us by God.” Χαρίζομαι — to give as a favour, gratuitously, the verb form of grace. One of the Spirit's main jobs is to help you understand what you have already been given.

scripture.text: Which things also we speak, not in words which man’s wisdom teaches, but which the Holy Spirit teaches, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things.
scripture.understanding: Paul's teaching came in words “which the Holy Spirit teaches” — διδακτός, taught, instructed. And then a phrase that can be read several ways: πνευματικοῖς πνευματικὰ συγκρίνοντες — “comparing spiritual things with spiritual things,” or “interpreting spiritual truths to spiritual people,” or “explaining spiritual realities in spiritual words.” All three are grammatically possible, and all three are true. The Spirit gives both the content and the vocabulary for it.

scripture.text: Now the natural man doesn’t receive the things of God’s Spirit, for they are foolishness to him, and he can’t know them, because they are spiritually discerned.
scripture.understanding: Ψυχικός — the “natural” man. Strong's notes it is built on ψυχή, the soul — life as it is lived at the level of ordinary human faculties. This person does not δέχομαι — welcome, accept — the things of the Spirit. They seem like μωρία, foolishness, to him. And he cannot know them, because they are ἀνακρίνω — examined, discerned — spiritually. This is not an insult to intelligence. It is a statement about faculties: you cannot see colour with your ears, and you cannot discern the things of God without the Spirit of God.

scripture.text: But he who is spiritual discerns all things, and he himself is judged by no one.
scripture.understanding: The spiritual person — πνευματικός, the one who has the Spirit — “discerns all things.” The same verb ἀνακρίνω. He can evaluate the world from God's perspective. But he “is judged by no one”: no merely natural person is in a position to evaluate him correctly. This is not a licence for spiritual arrogance — in chapter 3 Paul will tell the Corinthians they are not spiritual at all. It is a statement about where true discernment comes from.

scripture.text: “For who has known the mind of the Lord, that he should instruct him?” But we have Christ’s mind.
scripture.understanding: Paul quotes Isaiah 40:13 — “Who has known the mind of the Lord?” — which expects the answer: nobody. And then he gives the most astonishing answer in the chapter: “But we have Christ’s mind.” Νοῦς — mind, understanding, way of thinking. Not that believers know everything God knows, but that through the Spirit they have been given access to the way Christ thinks. And the mind of Christ, as this chapter has already shown, is the mind of the cross.

visualMeditations.title: The Man Who Arrived Shaking
visualMeditations.image: Picture the road from Athens to Corinth, about fifty miles along the coast. A man walks it alone, carrying his tools in a leather bag. He has scars on his back from Philippi. He has been chased out of Thessalonica and Berea. A few weeks ago he stood on the Areopagus in front of Stoic and Epicurean philosophers and some of them laughed at him when he spoke about a man raised from the dead. Now he is approaching the loudest, proudest, richest city in Greece. And he is afraid. Not mildly nervous — afraid, trembling, in weakness. He finds a tentmaking shop, rents a corner of it, and starts sewing leather.
visualMeditations.meaning: Paul does not hide this from the Corinthians; he reminds them of it. Why? Because he wants them to understand where their faith came from. It did not come from his brilliance — he had none to show them. It did not come from his confidence — he arrived shaking. It came from “demonstration of the Spirit and of power.” If you are waiting until you feel strong, articulate and confident before you share Christ, you are waiting for something Paul himself never had in Corinth. The gospel does not need your strength. It needs your obedience. The weakness is the very place where God's power gets the credit.

visualMeditations.title: The Rulers at the Foot of the Cross
visualMeditations.image: Picture the scene at Golgotha from the perspective of the powerful. Pilate washes his hands and signs the order, confident that he has kept the peace for Caesar. Caiaphas goes home satisfied that one man has died for the nation. Herod's soldiers have had their fun with a purple robe. Behind them all, the darkness — the principalities and powers Paul names elsewhere — rejoicing that the Holy One is dead. Every ruler of this age thinks it has won. And on the cross, unrecognised, hangs “the Lord of glory.”
visualMeditations.meaning: This is the hidden wisdom of God: the moment the rulers of this age thought they were destroying Jesus was the moment God was destroying their power. “For had they known it, they wouldn’t have crucified the Lord of glory.” They walked into God's plan with their eyes closed. And they are, Paul says in verse 6, “coming to nothing” — present tense, already in the process of collapse. Whatever power is pressing on you today, whatever system or authority or darkness seems to be winning, remember that every one of them is on a timer, and the cross has already set it.

visualMeditations.title: The Diver to the Bottom of the Sea
visualMeditations.image: Imagine standing on the deck of a ship over the deepest trench in the ocean, miles of black water below you. You want to know what is down there. You can lower a rope, but it runs out. You can shout, but nothing answers. You can study the surface for a lifetime and never see the floor. Then someone comes up from below — someone who has lived in those depths and knows every ridge and creature on the seabed — and climbs aboard and begins to describe it to you.
visualMeditations.meaning: That is the Holy Spirit. Βάθος — the depths — is the word Paul uses for “the deep things of God,” and the Spirit is the One who “searches all things.” No human method can reach the bottom of God: not philosophy, not religion, not experience. Only the Spirit, who knows God from the inside the way your spirit knows you from the inside, can tell you what is there. And here is the wonder of verse 12: He was given to you “that we might know the things that were freely given to us by God.” Most believers live their whole lives at the surface of what they have received. The Spirit wants to take you down.

structure.label: How Paul Preached in Corinth (v. 1-5)
structure.body: Paul recalls his arrival: no rhetorical superiority, a deliberate decision to know nothing but Christ crucified, personal weakness and fear, and a demonstration of the Spirit and power — so that their faith would rest on God, not men.

structure.label: God's Hidden Wisdom (v. 6-9)
structure.body: There is a true wisdom for the mature, but it belongs to God, not to this passing age. It was hidden, planned before the ages for our glory, and the rulers who crucified the Lord of glory never understood it.

structure.label: Revealed by the Spirit (v. 10-13)
structure.body: What no eye, ear or heart could discover, God has revealed through His Spirit, who searches His depths — and the Spirit both gives the truth and teaches the words to express it.

structure.label: The Natural Person and the Spiritual Person (v. 14-16)
structure.body: The person without the Spirit cannot receive or understand the things of God; the person with the Spirit discerns them — because believers have been given the mind of Christ.

sections.heading: Fear and Trembling in the City of Orators
paragraphs: To feel the force of verses 1 to 5 you need to know what a visiting speaker was expected to be in Corinth. Rhetoric was the great public art of the Greco-Roman world, and orators were celebrities. Crowds gathered to hear them the way modern crowds gather for concerts. They were judged on their delivery, their appearance, their voice, their elegance and their ability to move an audience — and they were paid accordingly. When Paul says he did not come with “excellence of speech or of wisdom,” he is describing a deliberate refusal to play that game. His critics in Corinth would later say exactly this about him: “his bodily presence is weak, and his speech is despised” (2 Corinthians 10:10). Paul does not dispute it. He says it was the point.

There is a popular interpretation that Paul had tried clever philosophy in Athens, failed, and therefore resolved in Corinth to preach only the cross. Be careful with it. Acts 17 does not record Athens as a failure — Dionysius the Areopagite, a woman named Damaris and others believed (Acts 17:34) — and the Areopagus speech is itself centred on repentance, judgment and the resurrection of Jesus. What is clear is that Paul arrived in Corinth bruised and afraid. He had been beaten in Philippi, driven out of Thessalonica and Berea, and mocked in Athens. And the Lord had to come to him in a night vision with words that only make sense if he needed them: “Don’t be afraid, but speak and don’t be silent; for I am with you” (Acts 18:9–10). The decision of verse 2 was not a change in theology. It was a decision about strategy, made by a frightened man who had concluded that the only thing worth risking his life on was the cross itself.

And notice why. Verse 5: “that your faith wouldn’t stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God.” Paul understood something that every age of the church has to relearn. Whatever you use to win people is what you must use to keep them. If you win them with brilliance, you will have to keep being brilliant, and they will leave for someone more brilliant. If you win them with entertainment, you will have to keep entertaining them. If you win them with the cross and the power of the Spirit, their faith will stand on something no rival can out-perform. Paul is not anti-intellectual — he wrote Romans. He is anti-dependency on the messenger. The aim of all true preaching is to make the preacher unnecessary to the hearer's faith.

sections.heading: Hidden Wisdom and the Rulers Who Did Not See It
paragraphs: Verse 6 makes a surprising turn. Having spent a chapter and a half attacking wisdom, Paul says, “We speak wisdom, however.” The Christian faith is not anti-wisdom; it is anti-pride. There is a wisdom so deep that it is reserved for the τέλειοι — the mature, those who are full grown. But it is a wisdom of a completely different kind from what Corinth valued. It is “not of this world,” and the rulers of this world do not understand it. It is μυστήριον — not a puzzle for clever people to solve, but a secret God kept and then chose to reveal. It was hidden, and it was planned “before the worlds for our glory” (v. 7). The cross was not God's emergency response to a plan that went wrong. It was His intention from before creation.

Who are “the rulers of this world” in verses 6 and 8? Honest readers divide. Some take them to be human authorities: Pilate, Herod, Caiaphas, the Sanhedrin — the people who literally crucified Jesus. Peter uses similar language in Acts 3:17: “I know that you did this in ignorance, as did also your rulers.” Others hear the spiritual powers behind those human rulers — the principalities and powers Paul names in Ephesians 6:12 and Colossians 2:15, where at the cross Christ, “having stripped the principalities and the powers, … made a show of them openly” (Colossians 2:15). The word ἄρχων is used of both in the New Testament (Jesus calls Satan “the prince of this world” in John 12:31 using the same word). The strongest reading is probably that Paul has both levels in view, the human rulers as the visible instruments of the invisible powers. Either way the point is spectacular: the authorities who crucified Jesus thought they were ending His influence, and they were in fact executing the plan of God that would end theirs.

Then verse 9, which is almost always misused. “Things which an eye didn’t see, and an ear didn’t hear, which didn’t enter into the heart of man, these God has prepared for those who love him.” People read it as a description of heaven — something so wonderful that we cannot even imagine it now. But verse 10 begins with “But”: “But to us, God revealed them through the Spirit.” Paul's point is not that we cannot know these things. It is that we could not have discovered them by eye, ear or heart — by observation, by tradition, by intuition — and that God has now revealed them by His Spirit. The things God has prepared for those who love Him are not only future. They include the gospel itself, the cross and its wisdom, which no human mind would ever have invented.

sections.heading: The Spirit Who Knows God From the Inside
paragraphs: Verses 10 to 16 give one of the clearest descriptions of the Holy Spirit's teaching ministry in the New Testament, and the argument is beautifully simple. Who knows what is going on inside a human being? Only that person's own spirit (v. 11). You can watch someone's face, hear their words and guess at their motives, but only they know their thoughts from the inside. In the same way, only God's Spirit knows the things of God. Which means that no human being, however brilliant, can reach into God's mind from the outside. Philosophy can speculate about God. Religion can reach towards Him. But only the Spirit of God can reveal Him, because only the Spirit knows Him from within. This is also, incidentally, one of the strongest statements of the Spirit's deity in Paul: the Spirit relates to God as a man's spirit relates to the man, and He searches “the deep things of God.” Nobody less than God can do that.

Then verse 14 introduces two kinds of people. The ψυχικὸς ἄνθρωπος — the “natural man,” the person living only at the level of ordinary human faculties — “doesn’t receive the things of God’s Spirit, for they are foolishness to him, and he can’t know them, because they are spiritually discerned.” This explains why intelligent people can look at the cross and see nothing but a dead man, and why some very simple people can look at it and weep with understanding. The issue is not intelligence; it is equipment. Spiritual things require a spiritual faculty to discern them, just as music requires hearing and colour requires sight. The person who has the Spirit — the πνευματικός — “discerns all things.” He has been given a new way of seeing.

And then the climax, the boldest phrase in the chapter: “But we have Christ’s mind.” Paul has just quoted Isaiah 40:13 — “For who has known the mind of the Lord, that he should instruct him?” — a question that expects the answer: no one. And Paul answers: we have. Not because believers have become omniscient, but because through the Spirit they have been given access to the way Christ thinks. But notice where this lands. Chapter 2 began with Christ crucified, and the mind of Christ is the mind of the crucified one — the mind Paul will describe in Philippians 2 as humbling itself, emptying itself, and becoming obedient to death. Having the mind of Christ does not make you superior to other people. It makes you willing to go lower than them. And that is exactly what Corinth, with all its spiritual gifts, did not yet have, as chapter 3 is about to make painfully clear.

ntConnection.heading: New Testament Connection
paragraphs: Jesus promised exactly the ministry Paul describes in verses 10 to 13. In the upper room He told His disciples: “But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you” (John 14:26). And again: “However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak. He will declare to you things that are coming. He will glorify me, for he will take from what is mine, and will declare it to you” (John 16:13–14). Notice how exactly that matches 1 Corinthians 2. The Spirit takes the things of Christ and reveals them; He does not speak on His own authority; He teaches the words. Paul's claim that he spoke “not in words which man’s wisdom teaches, but which the Holy Spirit teaches” (v. 13) is the fulfilment of that promise in the life of an apostle.

Verse 16 has a striking parallel in Romans, written a few years later from Corinth. At the end of his great argument about God's plan for Israel and the nations, Paul breaks into praise and quotes the same verse from Isaiah: “Oh the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past tracing out! ‘For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?’” (Romans 11:33–34). There, the quotation expresses the overwhelming mystery of God's ways. Here, it is answered: “But we have Christ’s mind.” Both are true at once. God's depths are unsearchable to human effort; and the Spirit who searches them has been given to us. Humility and confidence belong together in the Christian mind.

And the mystery of verse 7 is unpacked in Paul's later letters. To the Colossians he writes of “the mystery which has been hidden for ages and generations. But now it has been revealed to his saints, to whom God was pleased to make known what are the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory” (Colossians 1:26–27). That is the same word, the same hiddenness, the same revelation, and the same “glory” as 1 Corinthians 2:7. And in Colossians 2:3 he says of Christ: “in whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden.” The wisdom Corinth was looking for in orators and philosophers was hidden all along in a crucified Messiah. The world could not see it. The Spirit has shown it to you.

lexicon.insight: Strong's gives the simple sense “manifestation,” but in Greek rhetoric ἀπόδειξις was a technical term: the compelling proof that clinches an argument, the moment the orator's case becomes undeniable. This is its only appearance in the New Testament, and Paul uses it with deliberate irony. He refused the orator's tricks of persuasion (πειθός, “persuasive,” v. 4), and yet he says the Corinthians did receive an irrefutable proof — not of his skill but “of the Spirit and of power.” The proof that convinced them was not a better argument. It was God showing up. That is why their faith could stand “in the power of God” (v. 5).

Strong's: “a secret or ‘mystery’ (through the idea of silence imposed by initiation into religious rites).” Corinth knew this word from the mystery religions — the secret cults of Demeter, Isis and Dionysus, whose initiates were sworn never to reveal what they had seen. Paul takes the word and turns it inside out. In the New Testament a mystery is not a secret kept from people; it is a secret God has now chosen to tell. It was “hidden” and “foreordained before the worlds,” and now it is proclaimed openly to anyone who will listen. The gospel is not an exclusive club for the initiated. It is God's open secret, shouted from the rooftops.

Strong's: “to seek, i.e. (figuratively) to investigate.” The same verb is used of the prophets who “searched diligently” concerning the salvation to come (1 Peter 1:10 uses a compound of it), and of the Jews who “search the Scriptures” (John 5:39). Here it describes the Holy Spirit's relationship to God Himself: He “searches all things, yes, the deep things of God.” It does not imply that the Spirit is ignorant and needs to find out. It describes His complete, penetrating knowledge — the way a man's spirit knows the man (v. 11). And this is the One who has been given to you as your teacher.

Strong's defines ψυχικός as “sensitive, i.e. animate,” and explicitly distinguishes it “from G4152 (πνευματικός), which is the higher or renovated nature.” It is built on ψυχή, the soul — the natural life every human being has. The ψυχικός is not necessarily a wicked person; he may be cultured, religious and brilliant. What he lacks is the Spirit. Jude uses the same word for people who cause divisions: they are ψυχικοί, “sensual,” not having the Spirit (Jude 19). Paul's point is about capacity: without the Spirit, the things of God are not merely difficult; they look foolish. That is why the gospel must always be accompanied by prayer for the Spirit to open blind eyes.

Strong's: “the intellect, i.e. mind (divine or human; in thought, feeling, or will); by implication, meaning.” Νοῦς is the whole inner faculty of perception and judgment — not just intelligence, but the way you see, weigh and decide. In Romans 12:2 Paul says believers are transformed “by the renewing of your mind” — the same word. And in 1 Corinthians 1:10 he appealed to them to be perfected together “in the same mind.” Now he tells them what that one mind is: “we have Christ’s mind.” Unity in the church does not come from everyone agreeing with each other. It comes from everyone being conformed to Christ's way of thinking — which is the way of the cross.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with three things in this chapter: your belief that you must be impressive before God can use you, the foundation your own faith is actually standing on, and the depths of God you have been content never to explore.

items.title: You Do Not Have to Be Impressive
items.body: You have probably excused yourself from witnessing, serving, teaching or praying publicly because you are not good with words, not confident, not knowledgeable enough. Read verse 3 again: the apostle Paul arrived in Corinth “in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling.” He was not faking humility. He was afraid. And God built one of the most significant churches in the New Testament through a frightened man who refused to rely on his own polish. The Spirit is saying: your fear is not a disqualification. Your weakness is the stage on which His power gets the credit. What have you been waiting to feel strong enough to do? Do it in weakness this week.

items.title: What Is Your Faith Standing On?
items.body: Verse 5 is a diagnostic. Is your faith resting on the wisdom of men or on the power of God? Ask yourself honestly: if your favourite preacher fell into scandal tomorrow, would your faith shake? If someone presented you with an argument you could not answer, would you collapse? If your church split, would you stop following Christ? If any of those would topple you, your faith is standing partly on human wisdom — on a personality, a performance, an institution, an argument. The Spirit wants to move the foundation. Ask Him for a fresh encounter with the power of God, something no rival can out-argue and no scandal can undo.

items.title: Living at the Surface
items.body: The Spirit searches the deep things of God, and He has been given to you “that we might know the things that were freely given to us by God.” Yet most believers live their whole lives at the surface — a few familiar verses, a few routine prayers, a faith that never goes down into the depths. The Spirit is inviting you to dive. When was the last time you sat with a passage of Scripture until it opened? When did you last ask the Spirit to show you something about God you have never seen before, and then waited long enough for Him to answer? You have been given the mind of Christ. Do not leave it unexplored.

audit.title: The Foundation Check
audit.body: Write down the three things that most strengthen your faith. Then for each one, ask: is this the power of God, or the wisdom of men? A preacher, a book, an argument, a church community — these are good gifts, but if they are the foundation, your faith is vulnerable. If your list has no encounter with God Himself on it, ask why.

audit.title: The Weakness Check
audit.body: What is the one area where you feel weakest when it comes to serving God — speaking, praying aloud, explaining your faith, leading, giving? Write it down. Now ask: have I been treating this as a reason to hold back, or as a place where God could show His power? Paul turned his trembling into a testimony. What would it look like to do the same?

audit.title: The Natural-Mind Check
audit.body: Think of one area of your life — money, relationships, career, your body, your future — where you make decisions entirely by ordinary human reasoning and never ask what the Spirit says. That is where you are living as a ψυχικός, a natural person, even though you have the Spirit. Name it, and invite the mind of Christ into it.

practices.title: A Witness in Weakness
practices.body: This week, share something of Christ with one person in a way that feels weak to you. Do not prepare a polished argument. Before you go, pray verse 4 over yourself: “Lord, let my speech be not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power.” Then simply tell them what Jesus crucified means to you, in your own plain words. Afterwards, write down what happened — not whether they agreed, but what you noticed God doing.

practices.title: Diving With the Spirit
practices.body: Choose one short passage — 1 Corinthians 2:9–12 is a good one. Set aside thirty minutes. Read it slowly three times. Then pray: “Holy Spirit, You search the deep things of God. Show me what has been freely given to me.” Sit in silence for at least ten minutes. Write down anything that comes to you — a phrase that stands out, a connection, a conviction, a sense of God's love. Do not rush to conclusions. Repeat this practice twice more this week with the same passage, and notice how much more it opens each time.

prayerReflection: “Father, I confess that I have wanted to be impressive. I have measured myself by eloquence and confidence and knowledge, and I have held back from serving You because I felt weak. But Paul came to Corinth in weakness, in fear and in much trembling, and You built Your church through him. So I bring You my weakness today. I determine, like him, not to know anything except Jesus Christ and Him crucified. Let my faith not stand in the wisdom of men, but in Your power. Where my faith has been resting on personalities and arguments and performances, move it onto the rock of Your power. Lord of glory, the rulers of this age did not know You and they crucified You — and in doing it, they walked into Your plan. Thank You that every power pressing on my life is coming to nothing, and that You prepared glory for me before the ages. Holy Spirit, You search all things, even the deep things of God. I do not want to live at the surface of what I have been given. Take me down into the depths. Teach me what has been freely given to me. Open my eyes where I have been living like a natural man, deciding by my own reasoning without asking You. And thank You, Lord, that I have the mind of Christ — the mind that humbled itself and went to the cross. Let that mind be in me today. In Jesus' name, Amen.”

storyConnections.title: Moses and the Mouth He Did Not Trust
storyConnections.summary: At the burning bush, God commissions Moses to confront Pharaoh, and Moses produces excuse after excuse. Who am I? What will I tell them? What if they will not believe me? And finally the one that sounds most like Corinth's standards in reverse: he is not eloquent, he is slow of speech and of tongue. God's answer is not to make Moses a great orator. It is to remind him who made man's mouth, and to promise to be with his mouth and teach him what to say. When Moses still resists, God gives him Aaron — but the power that confronts Egypt is never Moses' rhetoric. It is the signs and the plagues and the parted sea. Paul stands in Moses' tradition: a reluctant, weak messenger, through whom God makes it unmistakable that the power belongs to Him.

storyConnections.title: The Night Vision in Corinth
storyConnections.summary: Luke gives us the scene behind Paul's “fear and much trembling.” Paul has come from Athens, and in Corinth he is working by hand as a tentmaker and preaching in the synagogue. When opposition rises he moves next door, but the threat does not go away. Then one night the Lord speaks to him in a vision: do not be afraid, but speak and do not be silent, for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many people in this city. Why would the risen Christ need to tell His great apostle not to be afraid? Because he was afraid. And the result of that word was eighteen months of ministry and a church that would outlast the empire. The courage did not come from Paul. It came from a promise spoken in the dark.

storyConnections.title: Unlearned Men Who Had Been With Jesus
storyConnections.summary: Peter and John are arrested after healing a lame man and are brought before the same Jewish rulers who had condemned Jesus. Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, preaches Christ crucified and risen to their faces. And Luke records the council's astonishment: when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled, and they recognized that they had been with Jesus. Two fishermen with no formal training silenced the educated elite — not by superior argument, but by the Spirit and by a healed man standing in front of everyone. That is 1 Corinthians 2:4–5 in a courtroom: the demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that faith rests on God and not on men.
